title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
description: Grade 12 Biology: structure of the flower, stamen and pollen grain, the pistil and embryo sac, and pollination, double fertilisation and seed and fruit formation.

topics.title: The Flower, Stamen and Pollen Grain
topics.concept:
The flower is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant (angiosperm). A typical flower has four whorls: the calyx (sepals), the corolla (petals), the androecium (the male part, made of stamens) and the gynoecium (the female part, the pistil). Sexual reproduction in plants involves the formation of male and female gametes and their fusion.

The stamen is the male reproductive part. Each stamen has a stalk (the filament) and a knob-like anther at the top. The anther usually has four pollen sacs in which the pollen grains develop by meiosis from pollen mother cells — this is microsporogenesis. Each pollen grain is the male gametophyte.

A mature pollen grain has a tough two-layered wall: the hard outer exine (made of a very resistant substance, sporopollenin, which protects it) and the inner intine. Inside, the pollen grain has two cells: a larger vegetative cell and a smaller generative cell. The generative cell later divides to form the two male gametes. Pollen grains are extremely well preserved (because of sporopollenin) and some people are allergic to them (causing pollen allergy).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the four whorls of a typical flower.
examples.solution:
A flower has four sets of parts.

  • Calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), gynoecium (pistil).

examples.problem: Example 2: What are the two parts of a stamen, and where do pollen grains form?
examples.solution:
The stamen is the male part.

  • It has a filament (stalk) and an anther.
  • Pollen grains form inside the anther's pollen sacs.
examples.answer: A stamen has a filament and an anther; pollen grains form inside the anther.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the function of sporopollenin in the pollen wall?
examples.solution:
Sporopollenin is in the exine.

  • It is a very resistant substance.
  • It protects the pollen grain (so pollen is well preserved).
examples.answer: Sporopollenin makes the exine extremely tough and resistant, protecting the pollen grain.

recap:
• Flower = reproductive organ; whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium (male), gynoecium (female).
  • Stamen = filament + anther; pollen grains form in the anther (microsporogenesis, by meiosis).
  • Pollen grain wall: outer exine (sporopollenin, tough) + inner intine; contains a vegetative cell + generative cell.
  • Generative cell → two male gametes.

quiz.q: Pollen grains are produced inside the:
quiz.explanation: Pollen grains develop inside the anther of the stamen.

quiz.q: The tough outer wall of a pollen grain, made of sporopollenin, is the:
quiz.explanation: The exine is the resistant outer wall made of sporopollenin.

topics.title: The Pistil, Ovule and Embryo Sac
topics.concept:
The pistil (gynoecium) is the female reproductive part of the flower. A pistil has three regions: a sticky top called the stigma (which receives pollen), a stalk called the style, and a swollen base called the ovary. Inside the ovary are one or more ovules, which after fertilisation become seeds.

Each ovule is attached to the ovary wall by a stalk (the funicle) and is covered by protective coats (integuments) that leave a small opening, the micropyle. Inside the ovule is a mass of tissue (the nucellus) containing the embryo sac — the female gametophyte.

The embryo sac develops by meiosis (megasporogenesis) and is usually 7-celled and 8-nucleate. Its important parts are:

  • The egg cell (female gamete), together with two helper cells (synergids), at the micropylar end — this group is the egg apparatus.
  • Three antipodal cells at the opposite (chalazal) end.
  • A large central cell with two polar nuclei in the middle.

So the female gametophyte is small but precisely organised, with the egg ready for fertilisation and the polar nuclei ready to form the food tissue of the seed.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three parts of a pistil.
examples.solution:
The pistil is the female part.

  • Stigma (receives pollen), style (stalk), ovary (contains ovules).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the embryo sac, and how many cells/nuclei does a typical one have?
examples.solution:
It is the female gametophyte.

  • The embryo sac is the female gametophyte inside the ovule.
  • A typical one is 7-celled and 8-nucleate.
examples.answer: The embryo sac is the female gametophyte; a typical one is 7-celled and 8-nucleate.

examples.problem: Example 3: Where is the egg cell located in the embryo sac, and what cells accompany it?
examples.solution:
The egg is at one end.

  • The egg cell is at the micropylar end.
  • It is accompanied by two synergids (forming the egg apparatus).
examples.answer: The egg cell is at the micropylar end, with two synergids forming the egg apparatus.

recap:
• Pistil: stigma (receives pollen) + style + ovary (holds ovules → seeds).
  • Ovule: covered by integuments with an opening, the micropyle; contains the embryo sac.
  • Embryo sac (female gametophyte): typically 7-celled, 8-nucleate — egg + 2 synergids (egg apparatus), 3 antipodals, central cell with 2 polar nuclei.

quiz.q: The part of the pistil that receives pollen is the:
quiz.explanation: The sticky stigma receives the pollen grains.

quiz.q: A typical embryo sac (female gametophyte) is:
quiz.explanation: The typical embryo sac is 7-celled and 8-nucleate.

topics.title: Pollination, Fertilisation and Seed Formation
topics.concept:
Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. When pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower (or same plant) it is self-pollination; when it is carried to the stigma of a different plant of the same kind it is cross-pollination. Cross-pollination is carried out by agents such as wind, water, insects and birds; flowers have many adaptations (bright petals, scent, nectar) to attract pollinators.

After pollination, the pollen grain absorbs water and germinates, growing a pollen tube down through the style to the ovule. The pollen tube carries the two male gametes and enters the embryo sac. Then a special event called double fertilisation takes place (unique to flowering plants):

  • One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote (this is syngamy). The zygote becomes the embryo.
  • The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei (the central cell) to form a triploid (3n) cell that becomes the endosperm — the food store for the embryo. This is triple fusion.

After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. The seed contains the embryo (with the future root and shoot) and a food supply, protected by a seed coat. The fruit protects the seeds and often helps in their dispersal. In this way one fertilised flower gives rise to seeds that can grow into new plants.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between self- and cross-pollination?
examples.solution:
It depends on where the pollen goes.

  • Self: pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower/plant.
  • Cross: pollen reaches the stigma of a different plant of the same kind.
examples.answer: Self-pollination is within the same flower/plant; cross-pollination is between different plants of the same kind.

examples.solution:
Two fusions happen.

  • One male gamete + egg → zygote (syngamy).
  • The other male gamete + two polar nuclei → triploid endosperm (triple fusion).
examples.answer: One male gamete fuses with the egg (zygote) and the other with the polar nuclei (3n endosperm) — two fusions, hence double fertilisation.

examples.problem: Example 3: After fertilisation, what do the ovule and ovary become?
examples.solution:
They develop into the seed and fruit.

  • The ovule becomes the seed.
  • The ovary becomes the fruit.
examples.answer: The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

recap:
• Pollination = transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; self vs cross (by wind, water, insects, birds).
  • Pollen germinates → pollen tube grows down the style carrying 2 male gametes.
  • Double fertilisation: male gamete + egg → zygote (syngamy); male gamete + 2 polar nuclei → 3n endosperm (triple fusion).
  • Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.

quiz.q: Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma is called:
quiz.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.

quiz.q: In double fertilisation, the endosperm formed is:
quiz.explanation: Triple fusion (male gamete + two polar nuclei) gives a triploid (3n) endosperm.

topics.title: Outbreeding Devices and Special Reproductive Modes
topics.concept:
Many plants actively avoid self-pollination because constant self-fertilisation reduces variation and vigour. To encourage cross-pollination, flowers use special arrangements called outbreeding devices:

  • Dichogamy — the anther and the stigma of a flower mature at different times, so self-pollen is not ready when the stigma is receptive.
  • Herkogamy — a physical or spatial barrier between anther and stigma (for example, they are placed apart) that prevents self-pollen from reaching the stigma.
  • Self-incompatibility — a genetic mechanism that prevents the pollen of a flower from fertilising the egg of the same plant, even if it lands on the stigma.

Some flowers are even unisexual, which makes self-pollination impossible. Cross-pollination is carried out by agents such as wind, water, insects, birds and even bats (large night-flowering blooms are often pollinated by bats).

A few plants reproduce in special ways that do not follow the normal seed-from-fertilisation route:

  • Apomixis — the formation of seeds without fertilisation. The seeds are genetically identical to the parent (useful for keeping a hybrid's good qualities).
  • Polyembryony — the occurrence of more than one embryo in a single seed (commonly seen in citrus fruits like orange).
  • Parthenocarpy — the formation of fruit without fertilisation; such fruits are seedless (for example, banana).

examples.problem: Example 1: What is dichogamy and how does it promote cross-pollination?
examples.solution:
It is a timing device.

  • The anther and stigma mature at different times.
  • So self-pollen is not available when the stigma is receptive, favouring cross-pollination.
examples.answer: Dichogamy is when the anther and stigma mature at different times, so self-pollen cannot be used and cross-pollination is favoured.

examples.solution:
Both skip normal fertilisation.

  • Apomixis: formation of seeds without fertilisation.
  • Parthenocarpy: formation of fruit without fertilisation (seedless fruit).
examples.answer: Apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation; parthenocarpy is fruit formation without fertilisation (seedless fruit).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is polyembryony? Give an example.
examples.solution:
More than one embryo per seed.

  • Polyembryony is the presence of more than one embryo in a single seed.
  • Example: citrus (orange).
examples.answer: Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a single seed, e.g. in citrus (orange).

recap:
• Outbreeding devices promote cross-pollination: dichogamy (different maturing times), herkogamy (physical barrier), self-incompatibility (genetic block).
  • Pollination agents include wind, water, insects, birds and bats.
  • Special modes: apomixis (seed without fertilisation), polyembryony (many embryos/seed — citrus), parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilisation — banana).

quiz.q: A genetic mechanism that stops a plant's own pollen from fertilising its egg is:
quiz.explanation: Self-incompatibility is the genetic block to self-fertilisation.

quiz.q: Seedless fruit formed without fertilisation, as in banana, shows:
quiz.explanation: Parthenocarpy is fruit formation without fertilisation (seedless).

questions.q: The male reproductive part of a flower is the:
questions.explanation: The androecium (stamens) is the male part.

questions.q: Each stamen consists of a filament and a/an:
questions.explanation: A stamen has a filament and an anther.

questions.q: Pollen grains are produced inside the:
questions.explanation: Pollen grains develop inside the anther.

questions.q: The tough outer wall of a pollen grain is made of:
questions.explanation: The exine is made of resistant sporopollenin.

questions.q: The female reproductive part of a flower is the:
questions.explanation: The pistil (gynoecium) is the female part.

questions.q: The part of the pistil that receives pollen is the:
questions.explanation: The stigma receives pollen grains.

questions.q: Ovules are found inside the:
questions.explanation: Ovules are enclosed in the ovary.

questions.q: The female gametophyte of a flowering plant is the:
questions.explanation: The embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

questions.q: A typical embryo sac is:
questions.explanation: The typical embryo sac is 7-celled and 8-nucleate.

questions.q: Transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower is:
questions.explanation: Pollen reaching the same flower/plant is self-pollination.

questions.q: Pollen reaches the ovule by growing a:
questions.explanation: The pollen tube grows down the style carrying male gametes.

questions.q: Fusion of a male gamete with the egg cell forming the zygote is called:
questions.explanation: Syngamy is the fusion of a male gamete with the egg.

questions.q: Fusion of a male gamete with the two polar nuclei forms the:
questions.explanation: Triple fusion gives the triploid endosperm.

questions.q: The two fusions occurring in flowering plants together are called:
questions.explanation: Syngamy plus triple fusion = double fertilisation, unique to angiosperms.

questions.q: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the:
questions.explanation: The ovary becomes the fruit; the ovule becomes the seed.

questions.q: The maturing of anther and stigma at different times to favour cross-pollination is:
questions.explanation: Dichogamy separates the timing of pollen release and stigma receptivity.

questions.q: Formation of seeds without fertilisation is called:
questions.explanation: Apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation.

questions.q: Pollen grains survive for thousands of years as fossils mainly because their exine contains:
options: Sporopollenin, one of the most resistant biological substances
questions.explanation: Sporopollenin resists acids, bases and high temperature, so pollen walls are extremely durable.

questions.q: Double fertilisation is considered unique because it produces both a:
questions.explanation: Two fusion events form the diploid zygote and the triploid nutritive endosperm — found only in angiosperms.

questions.q: Brightly coloured, scented flowers with nectar are usually adapted for pollination by:
questions.explanation: Colour, scent and nectar attract animal pollinators like insects and birds.

questions.q: The endosperm is important to the developing seed because it:
questions.explanation: The triploid endosperm stores food that nourishes the growing embryo.

questions.q: Cross-pollination promotes variation in offspring because it brings together:
options: Genes from two different parent plants
questions.explanation: Mixing genes from two parents increases genetic variation, unlike self-pollination.

questions.q: If the synergids guide the pollen tube into the embryo sac, removing them would most likely:
options: Hinder the entry of the male gametes
questions.explanation: Synergids help direct the pollen tube to the egg; without them, gamete delivery is impaired.

questions.q: Apomixis is useful in agriculture because the seeds it produces are:
options: Genetically identical to the parent, preserving hybrid traits
questions.explanation: Because no fertilisation occurs, apomictic seeds are clones of the parent, keeping desirable hybrid qualities.
